findings: adminRoutes.ts authorizes solely by reading the client-supplied request header `x-internal-role` (`req.headers['x-internal-role']`); HTTP headers are fully attacker-controlled and trivially spoofed by any caller (e.g. `curl -H 'x-internal-role: admin'`), so this is not an authentication check at all.

infra/network.yaml sets `public: true` on `api-service`, meaning the service backing `/admin/*` is reachable directly from the public internet — this directly contradicts the routes.yaml comment '# no auth middleware attached here; relies on the internal network for isolation', so the one security control the design depends on (network isolation) does not exist.

infra/routes.yaml attaches no auth/authz middleware to the `/admin/*` path at the gateway/infra layer, leaving 100% of admin authorization resting on the single spoofable header check inside the handler — defense in depth is absent.

Because the service is public and the role header is unauthenticated, any unauthenticated internet user can call POST /admin/refund with a forged `x-internal-role: admin` header and successfully trigger `processRefund`.
There is no verification that `orderId` in the request body belongs to any legitimate/authenticated account or session (no ownership/IDOR check), so an attacker can refund arbitrary order IDs.

There is no validation on `req.body.amount` (type, sign, or bounds) before passing it to `processRefund` — e.g. no check against the order's actual charged amount, no rejection of negative or zero values, allowing arbitrary/duplicate/over-refunds.

`processRefund(req.body.orderId, req.body.amount)` is called without awaiting a result or wrapping in try/catch, and the handler unconditionally responds `res.status(200).end()` afterward — if processRefund fails or throws asynchronously, the caller still receives a 200 success response with no error handling.

There is no audit logging of who performed the refund (no caller identity, no request source, no correlation ID) despite this being a sensitive financial operation — makes fraud undetectable and unattributable after the fact.
There is no rate limiting on the refund endpoint, so even a legitimate-looking automated caller (or the spoofing attacker) could issue unlimited refund requests.

The role check uses only a single flat string comparison (`role !== 'admin'`) with no signed/verifiable token (e.g., JWT, mTLS client cert, signed internal service token) — there is no cryptographic binding between the header value and any real identity or upstream gateway, so even if network exposure were fixed, nothing prevents header spoofing from any service on the internal network either.
